articles.title: Peter Max, psychedelic pop art icon, dies at 88
articles.summary: Peter Max, whose colorful, psychedelic pop art expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship, has died at 88, his son said in a written statement Wednesday.
articles.body: Peter Max, whose colorful, psychedelic pop art expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship, has died at 88, his son said in a written statement Wednesday. Max died on Monday, the statement said. No cause was given, but he had been suffering from advanced dementia. Max began his career in graphic design in the 1960s, and his swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs epitomized the era’s “flower power” art. But thanks to his prolific output and fun, accessible style, Max’s work remained popular well into the 21st century. Max was the official artist for the Olympics, the Super Bowl, the Indianapolis 500, the World Cup, the World Series and many other events. His art appeared on a Boeing 777 airplane and a Norwegian Cruise Line ship. His portrait subjects ranged from U.S. presidents to Taylor Swift. But in his first flush of success in the late 1960s and early 1970s, his murallike tableaus of flowers, the cosmos and cartoonish figures — all in vivid colors like turquoise, orange and neon green — seemed to be everywhere. Dorm room walls were plastered with his posters. Household furnishings like clocks and bedspreads sported his designs. He even created covers for the Manhattan Yellow Pages, a business phone directory distributed to millions of people. Max himself was featured on the cover of Life magazine in 1969, his trademark dark, bushy mustache framing a hearty grin. “We will remember his extraordinary creativity, his warmth, his curiosity, and the way he saw beauty and possibility everywhere,” his son Adam Max said in the statement announcing the death. “His art became part of American culture, but the man behind that art — the father we knew and loved — is the person we will miss most.” Family fled Nazi Germany Max was born Peter Max Finkelstein in 1937 to a Jewish family in Berlin. They fled Nazi Germany for Shanghai when he was a baby and later spent time in Tibet, Israel and Paris before settling in New York City when Max was 16. By then, he said in an interview, he was already “a huge fan of American culture”: comics, movies and “all the jazz music.” Max studied in New York at the Art Students League, the School of Visual Arts and Pratt Institute. In 1961, he opened a graphic design studio with friends. His bold, unique style was an immediate hit with ad agencies, publications, the corporate world and in pop culture. That led to a booming commercial business. “My work was really, I would say, almost exploited,” he said. “It was on mugs, it was on bedsheets, it was on dresses, it was on silks and scarves and ties — 70 product lines.” But what “bothered” him about all that success, he said, was that he “wasn’t painting anymore.” So he shut the business down for a time in the early 1970s to reconnect with his art. One of his biggest projects after returning to public life was a series of portraits of the Statue of Liberty, painted at the White House at the invitation of first lady Nancy Reagan in 1981. Max weathered various controversies in his personal and professional life. He pleaded guilty to tax fraud in 1997 after the IRS alleged he concealed more than $1 million in income from his art. He was originally sentenced to two months in prison but ultimately was allowed instead to serve the time in a work-release program, pay the back taxes and a $30,000 fine, and perform 800 hours of community service teaching art in Harlem schools. In 2015, his family life became tabloid fodder in a back-and-forth between his second wife, Mary Max, and Adam, his son from a previous marriage. The son and a guardian alleged that Mary Max had depleted his finances and browbeat him. She in turn claimed that they had kept him from her against his will and stolen paintings that belonged to her. Accounts of court appearances described him as frail. In 2019, Mary Max died by suicide two weeks after The New York Times published a story detailing legal battles over his work. His art had a bright, happy vibe Those dark allegations contrasted with the relentlessly bright, happy vibe that infused his work. “The colors are strong, sometimes loud, sometimes raw and sometimes harmonious, but always powerful, and the images are always on the side of the peaceful nature,” he said. “I don’t discuss in my paintings negative things, I don’t dwell on it in my mind and don’t dwell on it in my canvasses.” In another interview, he summed it up like this: “I see everything through rainbow eyes.” Although accounts of Max’s career sometimes lament that he was not taken seriously by the art establishment, in fact his work has been featured in dozens of museum exhibitions around the world. New York’s Museum of Modern Art owns seven of his works. The art for the Beatles’ “Yellow Submarine” is sometimes mistakenly attributed to Max, but the design for the album cover and “Yellow Submarine” movie are officially credited to the late Heinz Edelmann. Max claimed in a 2012 interview he did the original “Yellow Submarine” design before handing it off to Edelmann. But the website for New York’s Park West gallery, a longtime dealer of Max’s art, described Max’s involvement in “Yellow Submarine” as “early consulting work.” Max was, however, friends with the Beatles and many other celebrities. He also had a deep interest in Eastern spirituality. He brought “Swami” Satchidananda Saraswati to the U.S., and helped him popularize yoga here. Max’s first marriage to Elizabeth Nance ended in divorce. In addition to his son, he is survived by a daughter, Libra Astro.

articles.title: Why is Sneako suing Duel? Streamer reacts to controversial AI-generated casino video
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Sneako has threatened to take Duel to court after the crypto casino shared an AI-generated video that showed the streamer praying on a blackjack table.
articles.body: Sneako has threatened to take Duel to court after the crypto casino shared an AI-generated video that showed the streamer praying on a blackjack table. The clip quickly drew backlash because it mixed his Muslim faith with casino gambling. Sneako condemned the promotion publicly, while Duel later apologised and said the employee responsible for the campaign had been fired.Why is Sneako angry with Duel over the casino video?The controversy began after Duel published a promotional video featuring an AI-generated version of Sneako praying on a prayer rug placed on a blackjack table. The video also portrayed him thanking the platform for supposedly creating the "first halal casino."For Sneako, who has publicly identified as Muslim since 2023 and has frequently discussed Islam during his streams and interviews, the imagery crossed a clear line.On September 15, he reposted the video on X and strongly criticised everyone connected with the campaign, writing:"**** Duel casino and everyone affiliated. May Allah burn you all in the pits of hell."The streamer later addressed the situation during a Kick stream. His anger remained clear as he criticised the people involved in producing and approving the advertisement.He said:"All these people affiliated and working for Duel, may Allah burn you... May Allah torture you in the bottomless pits of Jahanam... I'm serious... I pray for your humiliation. I pray for your torture in the pits of hellfire."The dispute then moved beyond social media criticism. Sneako announced that he planned to pursue legal action against Duel and said he intended to use money received from the case for a project in Gaza.He wrote:"I am suing Duel for everything I can and using their ****** money to build another school in Gaza."Sneako has not publicly detailed the specific legal claims he intends to bring or confirmed that a lawsuit has already been filed.Duel apologises to Sneako and fires employee over AI advertisementThe controversy also drew a response from Clavicular, a fellow Kick creator and Duel's "Chief Inclusivity Officer." He publicly rejected the advertisement and said it was inappropriate to use someone's religion in this way.Clavicular wrote:"This is not cool to disrespect religion. Chief inclusivity officer here to disavow this tasteless video."He later said he called Sneako personally and apologised, adding:"Your religion shouldn't be disrespected."Clavicular initially claimed that the advertisement came from a "rogue agent" and said the people directly involved with Duel had not authorised it.He stated:"No one who's actually a part of Duel had anything to do with that campaign. It was a rogue agent."Duel's own statement offered a different explanation of the campaign's origin. The company accepted responsibility and said its content team had handled the advertisement from start to finish.Duel said:"We want to take this moment to apologize, unreservedly, for the absolutely tone-deaf edit of Sneako praying on a prayer rug that went out from our channels. This was executed end to end by our content team. That changes nothing about where responsibility sits."The company also confirmed that an employee named Nelli, who appeared to be responsible for the AI edit, had been fired.Duel added:"Mixing anything Islamic with the Duel Blackjack table was an absolute mistake. Nelli has been fired from Duel, effective immediately. To our Muslim friends, colleagues, and neighbors: like the faith you practice, we try to spread only peace and cohesion, and we deeply apologize for this transgression. We will keep a strict eye on quality control going forward to make sure nothing like this ever slips by again. Our own faith asks us to love our neighbor as ourselves. In this, we fell short. We are sorry."For now, the key question is whether Sneako follows through on his threat of legal action. Duel has apologised and taken internal action, but the streamer has indicated that the matter may not end with the company's response.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Republican congressman presses NHL over Alex Ovechkin’s appearance in Putin party campaign ad
articles.summary: Rep. Joe Wilson called Alex Ovechkin's appearance in a United Russia campaign ad "shameful" and urged NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman to review it.
articles.body: Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., has a problem with Alex Ovechkin appearing in a campaign advertisement for the Vladimir Putin-backed United Russia party, and he wants NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman to address it. Wilson sent Bettman a letter Tuesday calling the Washington Capitals captain’s participation "shameful" and asking the league to review the matter. Capitals owner Ted Leonsis was copied on the letter. Ovechkin does not speak in the ad. He stands behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in a United Russia campaign video ahead of Russia’s Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections. Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of the Russian state-controlled network RT, also appears in the ad. "While Mr. Ovechkin has every right to hold personal political views, actively participating in campaign material for Putin’s oppressive party while serving as the captain of an NHL franchise in our nation’s capital raises serious questions about the standards expected of players who represent the League and their communities," Wilson wrote. STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS POLITICS IS CAUSING 'DIVISION' WITHIN AMERICA'S LAST UNIFYING PASTIME The letter does not ask Bettman to suspend or fine Ovechkin. Wilson wants the NHL to explain whether it has any policies governing active players who appear in political advertisements for foreign parties or regimes. He also wants the league and Capitals to make clear that Ovechkin’s participation does not represent either organization’s position. Wilson was more direct on social media. "It is incredibly alarming that [the NHL] and [the Capitals] have allowed Alexander Ovechkin to appear in a campaign advertisement supporting the party of war criminal Putin," he wrote. "American hockey fans deserve better leadership from their star players!" Wilson elaborated on the letter Wednesday during an interview with Fox News’ Dan Scully. Asked what he wanted Bettman to do and whether he was seeking discipline for Ovechkin, Wilson did not directly answer. "For Ovechkin to be campaigning for a person who is indeed the new Hitler of the 21st century, it’s just inconceivable," Wilson said. Scully also asked whether Wilson had information that the NHL or Capitals knew about the advertisement beforehand. "Ahead of time, I’m not sure," Wilson said. Capitals respond to Ovechkin ad The Capitals said Ovechkin was approached while spending the offseason in Russia. "This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign," Capitals spokesperson Sergey Kocharov said in a statement to Reuters. But who asked him? The Capitals did not say. The team also did not answer questions from Fox News Digital/OutKick about whether it knew of Ovechkin’s participation beforehand or whether anyone within the organization approved or facilitated it. Kocharov noted that Ovechkin lives with his family in Moscow during the offseason and plans to return there after his NHL career. He said Ovechkin and the Capitals are focused on the upcoming season and his continued impact in Washington. WASHINGTON CAPITALS STAR ALEX OVECHKIN CRASHES A COUPLE'S WEDDING PHOTO SHOOT ON A HOTEL STAIRCASE Ovechkin has publicly supported Putin for years. He founded "PutinTeam" in 2017 to rally support for the Russian president, and his Instagram profile photo remains an image of the two men standing together. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin called for peace but declined to criticize Putin. "Well, he is my president," Ovechkin said at the time. "But, like I said, I’m not in politics. I’m an athlete." Wilson says Ovechkin should face ‘consequences’ Wilson argues that the Kremlin has a history of using athletes and international sporting achievements to promote the Russian government abroad. "An NHL superstar appearing in campaign propaganda for Putin’s political party cannot simply be dismissed as an activity wholly disconnected from the League," Wilson wrote. Wilson also writes that the broader United Russia campaign features Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights. The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Lvova-Belova and Putin in 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory. Scully asked Wilson how Ovechkin’s appearance differs from an American athlete supporting a U.S. politician. "The difference is that the American politician is not a mass murderer," Wilson said. "Now, we can all disagree," he continued. "There is a right to free speech, of course, but there should also be consequences of being associated in promoting a war criminal." Wilson did not say what those consequences should be. When Scully later asked directly whether he wanted the NHL to suspend Ovechkin, Wilson again did not answer. Wilson also said he is working with Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jim Risch, R-Idaho, and that Risch agrees Ovechkin’s participation "is just not right." Wilson did not describe what action, if any, he and Risch intend to pursue. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The congressman said he has not received a response from the NHL but is willing to give the league time to answer. Throughout the interview, Wilson repeatedly referred to Putin as a "convicted war criminal," echoing the handwritten message beneath his signature. The ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova in 2023, but neither has been convicted by the court.
